1. **p_5(Greta) vs. NL: Greta works on coastal conservation.** - Matches.
2. **p_4(Greta) vs. NL: Greta operates a submersible.** - Matches.
3. **¬p_3(Greta) vs. NL: Greta does not publish her research.** - Matches.
4. **¬p_2(Greta) vs. NL: Greta does not receive accolades.** - Matches.
5. **p_1(Greta) vs. NL: Greta will make new discoveries.** - Matches.
6. **p_0(Greta) vs. NL: Greta documents marine life.** - Matches.
7. **p_14(Greta) ⊕ p_5(Greta) vs. NL: Greta either explores the deep sea or works on coastal conservation, but not both.** - Matches, ⊕ correctly represents exclusive OR.
8. **∀x ((p_11(x) ∧ p_4(x)) → p_14(x)) vs. NL: For all x, if x maps the ocean floor and x operates a submersible, then x explores the deep sea.** - Matches.
9. **p_12(Greta) → p_1(Greta) vs. NL: If Greta analyzes ocean data, then she will make new discoveries.** - Matches.
10. **∀x ((p_10(x) ∨ p_12(x)) → p_13(x)) vs. NL: For all x, if x contributes to marine science or x analyzes ocean data, then x will advance our understanding of the climate.** - Matches.
11. **p_9(Greta) → (p_11(Greta) ∧ p_0(Greta)) vs. NL: If Greta collects seafloor samples, then she maps the ocean floor and documents marine life.** - Matches.
12. **∀x ((p_9(x) ⊕ p_8(x)) → p_10(x)) vs. NL: For all x, if either x collects seafloor samples or x explores underwater, but not both, then x contributes to marine science.** - Matches, ⊕ correctly represents exclusive OR.
13. **∀x (p_6(x) → p_7(x)) vs. NL: For all x, if x studies oceanography, then x gains knowledge about the marine world.** - Matches.
14. **¬p_6(Greta) vs. NL: Greta does not study oceanography.** - Matches.
15. **∀x ((¬p_9(x) ∧ ¬p_8(x)) → p_6(x)) vs. NL: For all x, if x does not collect seafloor samples and x does not explore underwater, then x studies oceanography.** - Matches.
16. **∀x (¬p_6(x) → ¬p_7(x)) vs. NL: For all x, if x does not study oceanography, then x does not gain knowledge about the marine world.** - Matches. This is the contrapositive of p_7(x) -> p_6(x), not p_6(x) -> p_7(x). This is a common logical fallacy called 'Denying the Antecedent'. If p_6(x) implies p_7(x), it does not mean that not p_6(x) implies not p_7(x). For example, if 'it is raining (p6) then the ground is wet (p7)'. If 'it is not raining (¬p6)' it doesn't mean 'the ground is not wet (¬p7)' (someone might have watered it).
